summary: The Guardian reports that lecanemab (Eisai) and donanemab (Eli Lilly), the first drugs to slow Alzheimer's by targeting amyloid, are expected to be considered for UK approval in 2024. Experts welcome them but stress they are not miracle cures, only slow progression by six months to a year in early-stage patients, and are costly and delivered by infusion. Slow, inadequate diagnosis, with long memory clinic waits and no widely available blood tests, is the major obstacle to patients getting treatment.
one_line: Lecanemab and donanemab, the first Alzheimer's drugs to slow disease, may reach UK approval review in 2024, but diagnosis delays and cost pose major hurdles.
key_facts: Lecanemab was recently approved in the US and Japan, and donanemab is expected to follow soon; UK authorities are expected to consider both for approval next year.
About a million people live with dementia in the UK, expected to rise to about 1.7 million by 2040.
Dementia killed 66,000 people in England and Wales last year and is the leading cause of death in Britain; Alzheimer's accounts for two-thirds of cases.
David Thomas of Alzheimer's Research UK said the new drugs slow Alzheimer's by six months to a year and are useful only in early stages, so they are 'certainly not miracle medicines'.
Alzheimer's is triggered by buildup of the protein amyloid in the brain, and scientists have tried for more than 20 years to stop it forming plaques.
Lecanemab is produced by Eisai and donanemab by Eli Lilly; both slow but do not halt progression.
The MHRA will decide whether the drugs are safe and effective, then Nice will rule on value for money.
Lecanemab costs about $25,000 (£19,700) a year and both drugs are given by regular intravenous infusions, which requires infusion suite space and time.
Memory clinic waits average up to two years, and about 65% of dementia cases are confirmed through the diagnostic process, while the remaining third are never diagnosed.
Mike Mackenzie-Smith's young-onset Alzheimer's took over 10 years and four tests between 2009 and 2017 to diagnose, when he was 65.
Trina Armstrong had symptoms from 2006, was wrongly told after a CT scan she probably had a stroke, and was later diagnosed with posterior cortical atrophy, a rare Alzheimer's variant.
Blood tests for Alzheimer's are under research but are several years from widespread use, according to Thomas.
Cath Mummery says Alzheimer's develops for at least 20 years before dementia and calls for brain health clinics to detect it earlier.
Researchers are developing active transport methods to get drugs across the blood-brain barrier, which could have a major impact.
